lesson.grammar_point: comparative structures and approximation for describing trends

vocab.title: Match each term to its meaning
defs: to decide which part of a budget goes where
the total cost of recruiting divided by the number of people hired
the starting figure that later numbers are measured against
what a current figure becomes if it continues at the same pace for a year
to reduce the effect of one cost or loss with a gain somewhere else
the rate at which people leave the company over a given period
an outside figure you compare your own number against
what you expect a number to be at a future date
the gap between what was budgeted and what was actually spent

paras: One sentence first, because everything below it is evidence for this and nothing else: we are not losing people to money, we are losing them in their first ninety days.

Attrition closed the quarter at fourteen per cent, three points higher than the same quarter last year and slightly above the market benchmark of around nine. It is not evenly spread. Two thirds of the leavers had less than a year of service, and more than half of those came from one site, where the shift pattern changed in May. Attrition among people with more than three years of service is flat.

Cost per hire is almost twice the benchmark. The reason is agencies rather than volume: we filled eleven roles through agencies in the quarter because the internal pipeline was empty, and each of those cost roughly three times an internal hire. The variance on the recruitment line is ninety thousand, marginally smaller than we forecast in March, and it is partly offset by a fall in overtime now that the two vacancies on the night shift are filled.

What we are doing about it, and who owns each: the onboarding redesign moves the training budget into the first ninety days, and Ana owns that with a December date. The shift pattern at the affected site is being reviewed with operations, and that one is not ours to close. At the current run rate we finish the year roughly eleven per cent over budget on recruitment, and I would rather flag that now than in November. The number I do not have yet is exit-interview data broken down by site.
reading.source: Alumni by Better -- internal note written for this lesson, with figures invented for practice

choices: Reporting every people metric of the quarter for the record.
Making one claim about why people are leaving, and defending it with figures.
Requesting an increase to the recruitment budget for next year.

items: Attrition is spread evenly across the workforce.
The note says it is not evenly spread: two thirds of the leavers had less than a year of service, and over half of those came from one site.
The high cost per hire is caused by the number of roles rather than by how they were filled.
The note says the reason is agencies rather than volume.
The recruitment variance came out smaller than the March forecast.
The note says ninety thousand, marginally smaller than we forecast in March.
The writer names an owner and a date for the onboarding work.
The note says Ana owns the onboarding redesign with a December date.
The writer claims to have complete data on why people left.
The note ends by saying the number not yet available is exit-interview data broken down by site.

items.situation: Say your attrition with the period and the comparison, in one sentence.
tips: Attrition closed the quarter at fourteen per cent, three points higher than last year.
Figure, period, comparison. In that order, in one breath.

items.situation: The CFO asks: compared to what? Answer.
tips: Slightly above the market benchmark of around nine.
Slightly, not a bit. And give the benchmark figure.

items.situation: Cost per hire is twice the benchmark. Say it and give the cause.
tips: Cost per hire is almost twice the benchmark, and the reason is agencies rather than volume.

items.situation: You are ninety thousand over on recruitment. Flag it before he finds it.
tips: The variance on recruitment is ninety thousand, partly offset by lower overtime.
The cause and the offset in the same sentence.

items.situation: He asks for a number you do not have. Answer in one sentence.
tips: I do not know, and I will have it by Thursday.
A date is what turns not knowing into a plan.

items.situation: Say the one sentence your quarter is really about.
tips: We are not losing people to money, we are losing them in their first ninety days.
One claim. Everything else is evidence for it.

listenings.text: People think I am listening for the number. I am not. I already have the number, it was in the file. What I am listening for is whether you know why it moved. If attrition goes from nine to fourteen and you tell me it went from nine to fourteen, you have told me nothing I did not have on Friday. Tell me it is concentrated in one site, that it started when the shift pattern changed, and that two thirds of the leavers had less than a year of service. Now I can do something. The second thing I listen for is whether you tell me the bad one before I find it. If I find it, I stop trusting the rest of the presentation, and that is not personal, it is arithmetic. And the third thing, honestly, is whether you can say I do not know. Nobody has ever lost credibility with me for saying I do not know and I will have it by Thursday.

My worst presentation had eleven slides and every one of them was true. That was the problem. Eleven true things is not an argument, it is a filing cabinet, and by slide four the room had gone quiet in the way that means nobody is listening. What I do now is decide the sentence before I decide the numbers. One sentence. Last quarter, ours was: we are not losing people to money, we are losing them to their first ninety days. Then every number I brought either supported that sentence or stayed at home. Three charts instead of eleven. And here is the part that surprised me. The questions got harder, not easier, because for the first time people understood what I was claiming and could argue with it. That is what you want. A room that argues with you is a room that heard you.
